analysis.one_liner: Charges fossil fuel producers a rising carbon fee and sends the money back to Americans as monthly dividend payments.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote; it sat in three House committees for 15 months until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a fee on the carbon content of coal, oil, and natural gas, starting at $15 per ton and rising each year. The money collected would go into a trust fund and be paid back to U.S. citizens and lawful residents as monthly dividend checks, one share per adult and half a share per child. It also includes border fees on carbon-intensive imports like steel and cement so American firms aren't undercut by countries with no carbon price, and rebates for farms and the military. Because everyone gets an equal dividend while wealthier households use far more energy on average, most lower- and middle-income households would come out ahead financially.
analysis.who_benefits: U.S. citizens and lawful residents receive monthly dividend payments funded by the carbon fee, with one full share per adult and half a share per child [S2][S3]. The dividend does not count as income for eligibility in federal assistance programs, so safety-net recipients get it on top of existing benefits [S3]. Households that use less than the average amount of fossil energy — typically lower- and middle-income households — receive more in dividends than they pay in higher fuel prices, because an equal per-person dividend redistributes from heavy energy users to light users. Clean energy industries gain as fossil fuels become more expensive relative to alternatives, and carbon capture facilities receive payments for sequestering carbon dioxide [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a carbon fee on producers and importers of crude oil, natural gas, and coal, starting at $15 per metric ton of CO2-equivalent and rising $10 per year, with faster increases if emissions targets are missed [S2][S3].

Deposits all fee revenue into a Carbon Dividend Trust Fund and pays it out monthly to every eligible adult and half-share per child under 19, with the first advance payment made the month before the fee takes effect [S3].
Counts the dividend only for the person receiving it — it is not treated as income or resources for any federal or federally funded benefit program, so it cannot push anyone off assistance [S3].

Adds border fee adjustments so imported fuels and carbon-intensive products like iron, steel, aluminum, cement, glass, and chemicals pay the same carbon cost as domestic production, protecting U.S. manufacturers from competitors in countries without carbon pricing [S3].

Sets an emissions reduction schedule targeting deep cuts from 2005 levels, and the fee is decommissioned once emissions fall below 10 percent of 2005 levels and dividends drop below $20 per month [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel producers — refiners, coal mining operations, natural gas pipeline suppliers, and fuel importers — pay the fee directly and would pass much of it through in higher prices for gasoline, heating fuel, and electricity [S2][S3]. Households that consume large amounts of fossil energy, and carbon-intensive manufacturers facing higher input costs, would pay more in costs than they receive in dividends. Administrative costs come off the top of the trust fund before dividends are paid [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and heavy energy users

drawbacks.text: A carbon fee raises gasoline, heating, and electricity prices, and while an equal dividend protects the average household, households with long commutes, inefficient homes, or high energy use could pay more than they receive in dividends, at least until payments begin up to 270 days after enactment [S2][S3].

Dividend payments are includible in gross income for tax purposes, and the fund covers its own administrative expenses — up to 8 percent in early years — before dividends are distributed, so some revenue never reaches households [S3].

The bill exempts agricultural fuel use and fuel used by the Armed Forces through full rebates, shrinking the emissions base covered by the fee and creating carve-outs that other fuel users ultimately fund [S3].

A carbon fee's effectiveness depends on regulators accurately measuring emissions and enforcing the border adjustments, and a good-faith critic would note that the bill relies heavily on Secretary discretion in identifying covered entities, products, and foreign carbon costs [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is one of the more consumer-friendly ways to price carbon: an equal dividend returned to every resident means most lower- and middle-income households come out financially ahead, and the dividend cannot affect benefits eligibility. The real costs fall on fossil fuel producers and on energy-intensive households and manufacturers, with border adjustments cushioning manufacturers against foreign competition. The main risks are price increases before the first dividend arrives, administrative leakage, and the agricultural and military exemptions. On balance the bill is a large, well-designed benefit for ordinary households at a substantial cost to the fossil fuel industry.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees in September 2023, then to subcommittees, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Salud Carbajal introduced the bill on September 27, 2023, joined by Rep. Scott Peters [S1][S3].
It was referred to the Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Foreign Affairs Committees, and later to subcommittees on Energy, Climate and Grid Security, Social Security, and Trade [S5].
The bill attracted 32 cosponsors, all Democrats [S4].
No committee ever reported the bill, and it never received a hearing, markup, or vote in either chamber before the Congress ended [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers and importers are better off: no carbon fee was ever imposed, and no dividends were ever paid. Heavy energy users also avoided higher fuel prices.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers dodged the fee

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 32 cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republican support, and the bill died in committee in a Republican-controlled House without a hearing or vote.

industries.note: Refiners, coal mining operations, natural gas pipeline suppliers, and fuel importers would pay the carbon fee directly and pass much of it through in higher energy prices. Their interest in stopping the bill ran directly against the dividend payments ordinary households would have received.

industries.industry: Clean energy and renewable power industries
industries.note: A rising carbon fee makes wind, solar, nuclear, and other low-carbon energy relatively cheaper, expanding their market. Cleaner air and slower climate change are public benefits that track the industry's growth.

Facilities that capture and sequester carbon dioxide would receive payments funded by the carbon fee. Whether this delivers real climate benefit depends on storage permanence, which the bill leaves to regulation.

industries.industry: Steel, aluminum, cement, glass, paper, and chemical manufacturers
industries.note: They would pay carbon fees on their energy use but receive refunds on exports and border fees charged to foreign competitors, largely shielding them from carbon leakage. Imported versions of these products would face new fees.
Farm fuel use is fully exempted through rebates, so farmers avoid the fee entirely while still receiving dividends.
Military fuel use is exempted through rebates, keeping the fee off defense operations.
